reference_title: Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-282, 2021)

sections.title: Deformation Equations: Axial Load and Bending
sections.summary: Axial deformation (Eq. 9-1); straight beam deflection as a bending term plus a shear term (Eq. 9-2) with Table 9-1's kb and ks and the section properties of Eq. 9-3 and 9-4; tapered beam shear deflection (Eq. 9-5) with the bending-deflection charts of Figs. 9-4 and 9-5; notches and holes; creep deflection.
sections.body: [p. 9-2] Equations for deformation of wood members are presented as functions of applied loads, moduli of elasticity and rigidity, and member dimensions. Average moduli of elasticity (E) and rigidity (G) are given in Chapter 5. Consideration must be given to variability in material. Axial load: the deformation of an axially loaded member does not usually take precedence over other loading, stability, or serviceability considerations. Axial load produces a change of length delta = P L/(A E) (Eq. 9-1), where delta is change of length, L initial length, A cross-sectional area, E modulus of elasticity (EL when grain runs parallel to member axis), and P axial force parallel to member axis. Straight beam deflection: the deflection of straight beams that are elastically stressed and have a constant cross section throughout their length is delta = kb W L^3/(E I) + ks W L/(G A') (Eq. 9-2), where delta is deflection, W total beam load acting perpendicular to beam neutral axis, L beam span, kb and ks constants dependent upon beam loading, support conditions, and location of point whose deflection is to be calculated, I beam moment of inertia, A' modified beam area, E beam modulus of elasticity (for beams having grain direction parallel to their axis, E = EL), and G beam shear modulus (for beams with flat-grained vertical faces, G = GLT, and for beams with edge-grained vertical faces, G = GLR). Elastic property values are given in Tables 5-1 to 5-5. The first term gives the bending deflection and the second term the shear deflection (Fig. 9-2). Values of kb and ks for several cases of loading and support are given in Table 9-1. I = b h^3/12 for a beam of rectangular cross section and pi d^4/64 for a beam of circular cross section (Eq. 9-3); A' = (5/6) b h for rectangular and (9/40) pi d^2 for circular cross section (Eq. 9-4), where b is beam width, h beam depth, and d beam diameter. If the beam has initial geometric imperfections such as bow (lateral bend) or twist, these imperfections could amplify deformations and lead to instability. Lateral or torsional restraints, therefore, may be necessary to hold such members in line. Tapered beam deflection: Figures 9-4 and 9-5, from Maki and Kuenzi (1965), are useful in the design of tapered beams. [p. 9-4] Tapered beams deflect as a result of shear deflection in addition to bending deflections, and this shear deflection can be closely approximated by Delta_s = 3 W L/(20 G b h0) for uniformly distributed load and 3 P L/(10 G b h0) for midspan-concentrated load (Eq. 9-5). The final beam design should consider the total deflection as the sum of the shear and bending deflections, and iterations may be necessary to arrive at final beam dimensions. Equations (9-5) are applicable to either single-tapered or double-tapered beams. As with straight beams, lateral or torsional restraint may be necessary. Effect of notches and holes: the deflection of a beam increases if holes or notches reduce effective cross-sectional dimensions; it can be determined by solving the differential equation of the elastic curve, EI(d2y/dx2) = M, for the variable cross section or by Castigliano's theorem. Creep deflections: wood beams and composite panels usually sag in time because of creep, which depends on magnitude and duration of the applied loads and the material rate of creep. Green timbers will sag if allowed to dry under load. If deflection under longtime load with initially green timber is to be limited, it has been customary to design for an initial deflection of about half the value permitted for longtime deflection. If deflection under longtime load with initially dry timber is to be limited, it has been customary to design for an initial deflection of about two-thirds the value permitted for longtime deflection.
key_points: Straight beam deflection: delta = kb W L^3/(E I) + ks W L/(G A'), Eq. 9-2, bending term plus shear term; kb and ks from Table 9-1 (p. 9-2)
I = b h^3/12 rectangular, pi d^4/64 circular (Eq. 9-3); A' = (5/6) b h rectangular, (9/40) pi d^2 circular (Eq. 9-4) (p. 9-2)
Tapered beam shear deflection: 3 W L/(20 G b h0) uniform load, 3 P L/(10 G b h0) midspan load (Eq. 9-5); bending deflection from Figs. 9-4 and 9-5; total is the sum (p. 9-4)
Creep: customary initial-deflection design of about half the permitted longtime deflection for initially green timber, about two-thirds for initially dry timber (p. 9-4)
sections.applicability: Serviceability (deflection) checks for axially loaded members and straight or tapered beams.

sections.title: Deformation Equations: Water Ponding, Combined Bending+Axial, Torsion
sections.summary: Ponding deflection Delta = Delta0/(1 - s/scr) (Eq. 9-6); deflection under combined bending and concentric axial load Delta = Delta0/(1 +/- P/Pcr) (Eq. 9-7) and eccentric axial load (Eq. 9-8); torsion, angle of twist theta = T L/(G K) (Eq. 9-9) with K = J for circular sections (Eq. 9-10) and K about h b^3/phi for rectangular sections (Eq. 9-11, Fig. 9-9).
sections.body: [p. 9-4] Ponding of water on roofs already deflected by other loads can cause large increases in deflection. [p. 9-5] Work by Zahn showed that the total elastic deflection Delta due to design load plus ponded water can be closely estimated by Delta = Delta0/(1 - s/scr) (Eq. 9-6), where Delta0 is deflection due to design load alone, s beam spacing, and scr critical beam spacing (Eq. 9-32). Combined bending and axial load: adding concentric axial load to a beam under bending loads increases bending deflection for added axial compression (Fig. 9-6) and decreases bending deflection for added axial tension. The deflection under combined loading at midspan for pin-ended, or simply supported, members can be estimated closely by Delta = Delta0/(1 +/- P/Pcr) (Eq. 9-7), where the plus sign is chosen if the axial load is tension and the minus sign if the axial load is compression, Delta is midspan deflection under combined loading, Delta0 beam midspan deflection without axial load, P axial load, and Pcr a constant equal to the buckling load of the beam under axial compressive load only and based on flexural rigidity about the neutral axis perpendicular to the direction of bending loads. If P is compression, it must be less than Pcr to avoid collapse. When the axial load is tension, it is conservative to ignore the P/Pcr term. If the beam is not supported against lateral deflection, its buckling load should be checked using Eq. (9-36). Eccentric load: an axial load eccentrically applied to a simply supported, pin-ended member at a distance e0 from the centroidal neutral axis (Fig. 9-7) induces bending deflections and a change in length given by Equation (9-1); the bending deflection is found by writing Equation (9-7) in the form delta_b + e0 = e0/(1 +/- P/Pcr) (Eq. 9-8), where delta_b is the induced bending deflection at midspan. Torsion: the angle of twist of wood members about the longitudinal axis is theta = T L/(G K) (Eq. 9-9), where theta is angle of twist in radians, T applied torque, L member length, G shear modulus (use the square root of GLR GLT, or approximate G by EL/16 if measured G is not available), and K a torsional constant dependent on cross-sectional shape. For a circular cross section, K equals the polar moment of inertia J = pi D^4/32 (Eq. 9-10). For noncircular cross sections, which warp under torsion, empirical methods can be used; for a rectangular cross section K = J approximately h b^3/phi (Eq. 9-11), where h is the larger cross-section dimension, b the smaller, and phi is given in Figure 9-9.
key_points: Ponding: Delta = Delta0/(1 - s/scr), Eq. 9-6, scr from Eq. 9-32 (p. 9-5)

Combined bending and axial load: Delta = Delta0/(1 +/- P/Pcr), Eq. 9-7, plus for tension, minus for compression; in compression P must be less than Pcr to avoid collapse; for tension it is conservative to ignore P/Pcr (p. 9-5)
A beam not supported against lateral deflection should have its buckling load checked with Eq. 9-36 (p. 9-5)
Torsion: theta = T L/(G K), Eq. 9-9; G = square root of GLR GLT, or EL/16 if measured G is not available; K = pi D^4/32 circular (Eq. 9-10), about h b^3/phi rectangular (Eq. 9-11, Fig. 9-9) (p. 9-5)
sections.applicability: Roof ponding stability checks, beam-column deflection under combined loading, and torsional deformation of members.

sections.title: Stress Equations: Axial Load and Straight Beam Stresses
sections.summary: Uniform axial stress ft = P/A (Eq. 9-12), also used for short-block compression; bending stress fb = M/S at the extreme fibers (Eq. 9-13), which with the ultimate moment gives the modulus of rupture; maximum beam shear stress fv = k V/A (Eq. 9-14, k = 3/2 rectangular, 4/3 circular).
sections.body: [p. 9-5] The stress equations are limited by the assumption that stress and strain are directly proportional (Hooke's law) and by the fact that local stresses in the vicinity of points of support or points of load application are correct only to the extent of being statically equivalent to the true stress distribution (St. Venant's principle). [p. 9-6] Local stress concentrations must be separately accounted for if they are to be limited in design. Concentric axial load produces a uniform stress ft = P/A (Eq. 9-12), where ft is tensile stress, P axial load, and A cross-sectional area. Equation (9-12) can also be used in compression; if the member under compression is short enough to fail by fiber crushing without suddenly deflecting laterally or buckling, this uniform stress state will prevail until the member is loaded to material capacity. Bending: the strength of beams is determined by flexural stresses caused by bending moment, shear stresses caused by shear load, and compression across the grain at the end bearings and load points. [p. 9-7] The maximum stress, at extreme top and bottom fibers of the cross section, is fb = M/S (Eq. 9-13), where fb is bending stress, M bending moment, and S beam section modulus (for a rectangular cross section, S = b h^2/6; for a circular cross section, S = pi D^3/32). [p. 9-8] Equation (9-13) is also used beyond the limits of Hooke's law with M as the ultimate moment at failure; the resulting pseudo-stress is called the modulus of rupture, values of which are tabulated in Chapter 5. The modulus of rupture has been found to decrease with increasing size of member. For beams of uniform cross section, the shear stress due to bending is a maximum at the neutral axis (not true if the beam is tapered). The maximum shear stress acting on a beam cross section is fv = k V/A (Eq. 9-14), where fv is shear stress, V vertical shear force on cross section, A cross-sectional area, and k = 3/2 for a rectangular cross section or k = 4/3 for a circular cross section. Equation 9-14 is intended for beams with solid cross sections. For an I-shape, the shear capacity of the cross section is conservatively estimated by the rectangular web. For long beams, the load capacity is limited by bending moment capacity and Equation (9-13) governs design; for short beams, shear limits the load capacity because wood is relatively weak in shear strength (Soltis and Rammer (1997) tabulate span-to-depth ratios where shear is likely to limit capacity).
key_points: Axial stress ft = P/A, Eq. 9-12, also used in compression for a member short enough to fail by fiber crushing without buckling (p. 9-6)
Local stress concentrations must be separately accounted for if they are to be limited in design (p. 9-6)
Bending stress fb = M/S, Eq. 9-13; with the ultimate moment it gives the modulus of rupture (p. 9-7, 9-8)
Shear stress fv = k V/A, Eq. 9-14, k = 3/2 rectangular, 4/3 circular; for solid cross sections; for an I-shape conservatively estimated by the rectangular web (p. 9-8)
sections.applicability: The fundamental axial, bending, and shear stress checks for straight members of uniform section.

sections.title: Stress Equations: Tapered Beam Stresses
sections.summary: Tapered beams of constant width tapering in depth at less than 25 degrees: bending stress from Eq. 9-13 within 5%, but a different shear stress; the combined stresses at the tapered edge (Eq. 9-16: fx = 3M/(2 b h0^2), fxy = fx tan(theta), fy = fx tan^2(theta)) checked by the Norris interaction equation (Eq. 9-15).
sections.body: [p. 9-8] For beams of constant width that taper in depth at a slope less than 25 degrees, the bending stress can be obtained from Equation (9-13) with an error of less than 5%. The shear stress, however, differs markedly from that found in uniform beams; it can be determined from the basic theory presented by Maki and Kuenzi (1965). [p. 9-9] The shear stress at the tapered edge can reach a maximum value as great as that at the neutral axis at a reaction. For the beam depicted in Figure 9-12, the bending and shear combine to produce a maximum tension stress at point O. The effect of combined stresses at point O can be approximated by an interaction equation based on the Henky-von Mises theory of energy due to the change of shape, which Norris (1950) applied to wood: fx^2/Fx^2 + fxy^2/Fxy^2 + fy^2/Fy^2 = 1 (Eq. 9-15), [p. 9-10] where fx is bending stress, fy stress perpendicular to the neutral axis, and fxy shear stress; values of Fx, Fy, and Fxy are corresponding stresses chosen at design values or maximum values in accordance with allowable or maximum values being determined for the tapered beam. Maximum stresses in the beam of Figure 9-12 are fx = 3M/(2 b h0^2), fxy = fx tan(theta), fy = fx tan^2(theta) (Eq. 9-16). Substitution of these equations into Equation (9-15) results in an expression for the moment capacity M of the beam. If the taper is on the beam tension edge, the values of fx and fy are tensile stresses; if a beam is tapered along the compression flange, the orientation of forces acting perpendicular to grain reverses. Example: Determine the moment capacity (newton-meters) of a tapered beam of width b = 100 mm, depth h0 = 200 mm, and taper tan theta = 1/10. Substituting these dimensions into Equation (9-16) (with stresses in pascals) results in fx = 375M, fxy = 37.5M, fy = 3.75M. Substituting these into Equation (9-15) and solving for M results in M = 1/(3.75 [10^4/Fx^2 + 10^2/Fxy^2 + 1/Fy^2]^(1/2)), where appropriate allowable or maximum values of the F stresses (pascals) are based on test data.
key_points: For constant-width beams tapered at less than 25 degrees, bending stress from Eq. 9-13 is within 5%, but shear stress differs markedly from uniform beams (p. 9-8)
Norris interaction: fx^2/Fx^2 + fxy^2/Fxy^2 + fy^2/Fy^2 = 1, Eq. 9-15 (p. 9-9)
Tapered-edge stresses: fx = 3M/(2 b h0^2), fxy = fx tan(theta), fy = fx tan^2(theta), Eq. 9-16; substituted in Eq. 9-15 they give the moment capacity (p. 9-10)
sections.applicability: Checking tapered glulam or sawn beams for combined stress at the tapered edge (a location often overlooked if only Eq 9-13 bending stress is checked).

sections.title: Stress Equations: Size Effect
sections.summary: Modulus of rupture decreases as beam size increases (weakest-link statistical strength theory): the two-point-loading ratio (Eq. 9-17, m = 18 for clear Douglas-fir), its form against a 50.8 mm deep, 711.12 mm span midspan-loaded beam (Eq. 9-18a/b), uniform versus concentrated load (Eq. 9-19), and beam shear strength from ASTM D143 shear blocks (Eq. 9-20a/b).
sections.body: [p. 9-10] The modulus of rupture (maximum bending stress) of wood beams depends on beam size and method of loading. The strength of clear, straight-grained beams generally decreases as size increases. Bohannan (1966) shows that this size effect can be modeled by statistical strength theory. For two beams under two equal concentrated loads applied symmetrical to the midspan points (Fig. 9-13a), the ratio of the modulus of rupture of beam 1 to beam 2 is R1/R2 = [h2 L2 (1 + m a2/L2)/(h1 L1 (1 + m a1/L1))]^(1/m) (Eq. 9-17), where R is modulus of rupture, h beam depth, L beam span, a distance between loads placed a/2 each side of midspan, and m an empirically determined material constant. For clear, straight-grained Douglas-fir beams, Bohannan (1966) analyzed three sets of data and determined m = 18. If beam 2 is loaded at midspan (a2 = 0) with h2 = 50.8 mm (2 in.) and L2 = 711.12 mm (28 in.), Equation (9-17) becomes R1 = R2 [36125/(h1 L1 (1 + m a1/L1))]^(1/m) (Eq. 9-18a, printed with the label MPa) and R1 = R2 [56/(h1 L1 (1 + m a1/L1))]^(1/m) (lbf in^-2) (Eq. 9-18b). The printed example: a beam 10 in. deep, spanning 18 ft, loaded at one-third span points, compared with a beam 2 in. deep, spanning 28 in., loaded at midspan with a modulus of rupture of 10,000 lbf in^-2, m = 18: R1 = 10,000 [56/(2,160(1 + 6))]^(1/18) = 7,330 lbf in^-2. Liu (1982) extended the theory to uniform, singly and doubly tapered beams of rectangular cross section under uniformly distributed load; [p. 9-11] for a beam of uniform rectangular cross section, Ru/Rc = [(1 + 18 ac/Lc) hc Lc/(3.876 hu Lu)]^(1/18) (Eq. 9-19), where subscripts u and c refer to beams under uniformly distributed and concentrated loads; m was determined as 18 by fitting data to multiple experiments with Douglas-fir beams. Shear strength for non-split, non-checked, solid-sawn, and glulam beams also decreases as beam size increases (Liu 1980): tau = 1.9 Cf tau_ASTM/A^(1/5) (metric) (Eq. 9-20a), tau = 1.3 Cf tau_ASTM/A^(1/5) (inch-pound) (Eq. 9-20b), where tau is beam shear (MPa, lb in^-2), Cf stress concentration factor, tau_ASTM ASTM D143 shear block strength (MPa, lb in^-2), and A shear area (cm^2, in^2). The shear block re-entrant corner concentration factor is approximately 2; the shear area is defined as beam width multiplied by the length of beam subjected to shear force.
key_points: Size effect, two-point loading: R1/R2 = [h2 L2 (1 + m a2/L2)/(h1 L1 (1 + m a1/L1))]^(1/m), Eq. 9-17; m = 18 for clear, straight-grained Douglas-fir (p. 9-10)
Printed example of Eq. 9-18b: 10 in. deep, 18 ft span, third-point loads against a 2 in., 28 in., midspan beam at 10,000 lbf in^-2 gives 7,330 lbf in^-2 (p. 9-10)
Uniform versus concentrated load: Ru/Rc = [(1 + 18 ac/Lc) hc Lc/(3.876 hu Lu)]^(1/18), Eq. 9-19 (p. 9-11)
Beam shear: tau = 1.9 Cf tau_ASTM/A^(1/5) (metric, A in cm^2), Eq. 9-20a; 1.3 (inch-pound), Eq. 9-20b; Cf approximately 2 (p. 9-11)
sections.applicability: Adjusting clear-wood strength test data (or design values derived from it) for the actual member size being designed.

sections.title: Stress Equations: Effect of Notches, Slits, and Holes
sections.summary: Sharp interior corners at notches, slits, or holes cause stress concentrations that can initiate a crack along the grain; a conservative crack-initiation criterion for a beam with a slit, sqrt(h)[A(6M/(b h^2)) + B(3V/(2 b h))] = 1 (Eq. 9-21), with A and B from Figure 9-14.
sections.body: [p. 9-11] In beams having notches, slits, or holes with sharp interior corners, large stress concentrations exist at the corners. The local stresses include shear parallel to grain and tension perpendicular to grain. As a result, even moderately low [p. 9-12] loads can cause a crack to initiate at the sharp corner and propagate along the grain. An estimate of the crack-initiation load can be obtained by the fracture mechanics analysis of Murphy (1979) for a beam with a slit, but it is generally more economical to avoid sharp notches entirely in wood beams. Sharp notches cause greater reductions in strength for larger beams, resulting from size effects. A conservative criterion for crack initiation for a beam with a slit is sqrt(h) [A (6M/(b h^2)) + B (3V/(2 b h))] = 1 (Eq. 9-21), where h is beam depth, b beam width, M bending moment, and V vertical shear force, and coefficients A and B are presented in Figure 9-14 as functions of a/h, where a is slit depth. The value of A depends on whether the slit is on the tension edge or the compression edge; therefore, use either At or Ac as appropriate. The values of A and B are dependent upon species. The values given in Figure 9-14, however, are conservative for most softwood species. Creep rupture is accounted for by duration-of-load adjustment in the setting of allowable stresses (Chapters 5 and 7); ponding increases bending stresses by the same amplification factor (Eq. 9-6) used with deflection.
key_points: It is generally more economical to avoid sharp notches entirely in wood beams; sharp notches cause greater strength reductions in larger beams (p. 9-12)
Crack initiation for a beam with a slit: sqrt(h)[A(6M/(b h^2)) + B(3V/(2 b h))] = 1, Eq. 9-21; A (At or Ac) and B from Figure 9-14 against a/h; conservative for most softwood species (p. 9-12)
Ponding increases bending stresses by the same amplification factor as deflection, Eq. 9-6 (p. 9-12)
sections.applicability: Checking beams with end notches, bolt holes, or other sharp-cornered cross-section reductions.

sections.title: Stress Equations: Combined Bending and Axial Load, Torsion
sections.summary: Bending stress under combined bending and concentric axial load fb = fb0/(1 +/- P/Pcr) (Eq. 9-22), superposed on P/A; eccentric axial load adds +/-P e0/S to fb0; torsional shear stress fs = 16T/(pi d^3) for circular sections (Eq. 9-23) and fs = T/(beta h b^2) for rectangular sections (Eq. 9-24, beta from Fig. 9-15; as printed; see the note in the body: with beta dividing, the stress comes out 9 to 23 times too small).
sections.body: [p. 9-12] Equation (9-7) gives the effect on deflection of adding an axial end load to a simply supported pin-ended beam already bent by transverse flexural loads. The bending stress in the member is modified by the same factor: fb = fb0/(1 +/- P/Pcr) (Eq. 9-22), where the plus sign is chosen if the axial load is tension and the minus sign if the axial load is compression, fb is net bending stress from combined bending and axial load, fb0 bending stress without axial load, P axial load, and Pcr the buckling load of the beam under axial compressive load only. This Pcr is not necessarily the minimum buckling load of the member; if the axial load is compressive, the possibility of buckling under combined loading must be checked (Interaction of Buckling Modes). The total stress under combined bending and axial load is obtained by superposition of the stresses given by Equations (9-12) and (9-22). Example: Suppose transverse loads produce a bending stress fb0 tensile on the convex edge and compressive on the concave edge of the beam. Then the addition of a tensile axial force P at the centroids of the end sections will produce a maximum tensile stress on the convex edge of ft max = fb0/(1 + P/Pcr) + P/A and a maximum compressive stress on the concave edge of fc max = fb0/(1 + P/Pcr) - P/A, where a negative result would indicate that the stress was in fact tensile. Eccentric Load. If the axial load is eccentrically applied, then the bending stress fb0 should be augmented by +/-P e0/S, where e0 is eccentricity of the axial load. If applied in a manner that creates a convex curvature, opposite to that shown in Figure 9-7, then e0 is negative. Example: In the preceding example, let the axial load be eccentric with respect to the concave edge of the beam, as shown in Figure 9-7. Then the maximum stresses become ft max = (fb0 - P e0/S)/(1 + P/Pcr) + P/A and fc max = (fb0 - P e0/S)/(1 + P/Pcr) - P/A. Torsion: for a circular cross section, the shear stress induced by torsion is fs = 16T/(pi d^3) (Eq. 9-23), where T is the applied torsional moment and d diameter. [p. 9-13] For a rectangular cross section, fs = T/(beta h b^2) (Eq. 9-24), where h is the larger cross-section dimension, b the smaller, and beta is presented in Figure 9-15. Print note: Figure 9-15 gives beta from 3 (b/h = 0) to about 4.8 (b/h = 1), the values of the multiplier in fs = beta T/(h b^2); read with beta dividing as printed, Eq. 9-24 gives a stress about 9 to 23 times smaller.
key_points: Combined bending and axial load: fb = fb0/(1 +/- P/Pcr), Eq. 9-22, superposed with P/A (Eq. 9-12); with compressive axial load, buckling under combined loading must be checked (p. 9-12)
Eccentric axial load: fb0 is augmented by +/-P e0/S before the amplification (p. 9-12)
Torsion, circular: fs = 16T/(pi d^3), Eq. 9-23 (p. 9-12)

Torsion, rectangular: printed fs = T/(beta h b^2), Eq. 9-24, beta from Figure 9-15 (3 to about 4.8); with beta dividing as printed the stress is 9 to 23 times smaller than fs = beta T/(h b^2) (p. 9-13)
sections.applicability: Beam-columns (combined axial + bending) and members under torsion, e.g. eccentrically loaded posts or out-of-plane-loaded beams.

sections.title: Stability Equations: Axial Compression (Long and Short Columns)
sections.summary: Columns: long columns by Euler's formula fcr = pi^2 EL/(L/r)^2 (Eq. 9-25, r from Eq. 9-26); short columns by the FPL fourth-power formula (Eq. 9-27) or Ylinen's buckling equation (Eq. 9-28, 9-29; c = 0.8 solid-sawn and glulam, 0.9 structural composite lumber); built-up columns with Kf (Eq. 9-30); spaced columns; flange instability fcr = 0.044 E t^2/b^2 (Eq. 9-31).
sections.body: [p. 9-13] For slender members under axial compression, a sudden loss of stability is the principal failure mode. The equations are for concentrically loaded members; for eccentrically loaded columns, see Interaction of Buckling Modes. A column long enough to buckle before the compressive stress P/A exceeds the proportional limit stress is a long column; the critical stress at buckling is fcr = pi^2 EL/(L/r)^2 (Eq. 9-25), where EL is elastic modulus parallel to the axis of the member, L unbraced length, and r least radius of gyration, r = sqrt(I/A) (Eq. 9-26). Equation (9-25) is based on an idealized pinned-end condition (Fig. 9-17a); end moments that a column with squared-off ends bearing on a rigid surface may develop are conservatively neglected. Columns that buckle at a compressive stress beyond the proportional limit stress are short columns. Newlin and Gahagan (1930) give a fourth-power parabolic function, fcr = Fc [1 - (4/(27 pi^4)) ((L/r) sqrt(Fc/EL))^4] (Eq. 9-27), where Fc is compressive strength (Fig. 9-18). [p. 9-14] Ylinen's nonlinear stress-strain function, epsilon = (Fc/EL)[c f/Fc - (1 - c) ln(1 - f/Fc)] (Eq. 9-28), with c a constant between 0 and 1, leads to Ylinen's buckling equation fcr = (Fc + fe)/(2c) - sqrt([(Fc + fe)/(2c)]^2 - Fc fe/c) (Eq. 9-29), where fe is the buckling stress given by Euler's formula. Equation (9-29) agrees closely with the FPL fourth-power formula if c = 0.957. Comparing the fourth-power parabolic function to experimental data indicates that the function is nonconservative for intermediate L/r range columns. Using Ylinen's buckling equation with c = 0.8 gives a better estimate for the solid-sawn and glued-laminated data, whereas c = 0.9 gives a better estimate for structural composite lumber. Built-up columns of nearly square cross section cannot support as much load as a solid or glue-laminated column of similar dimensions, because the dowel-type fasteners that hold the cross section together deform and slip. If built-up columns are adequately connected and the axial load is near the geometric center of the cross section, the capacity is Equation (9-29) reduced by Kf: fcr = Kf [(Fc + fe)/(2c) - sqrt([(Fc + fe)/(2c)]^2 - Fc fe/c)] (Eq. 9-30), where Kf is the built-up stability factor: for bolts, Kf = 0.75, and for nails, Kf = 0.6, provided bolt and nail spacing requirements meet design specification approval. Spacer blocks of spaced columns should be placed close enough together that the unsupported portion of the spaced member will not locally buckle at the same or lower stress than the complete member; spaced columns are designed considering each compression member as an unsupported simple column, the sum of their loads being the column load. Columns with thin, outstanding flanges (I, H, +, L sections, Fig. 9-20) can fail by elastic instability of the outstanding flange at stresses less than those for general column instability; Trayer and March (1931) estimated the flange instability stress by fcr = 0.044 E t^2/b^2 (Eq. 9-31), where E is column modulus of elasticity, t thickness of the outstanding flange, and b its width. [p. 9-15] If the joints between the column members are glued and reinforced with glued fillets, the instability stress increases to as much as 1.6 times that given by Equation (9-31).
key_points: Long columns: Euler fcr = pi^2 EL/(L/r)^2, Eq. 9-25, r = sqrt(I/A), Eq. 9-26 (p. 9-13)

The FPL fourth-power formula (Eq. 9-27) is nonconservative for intermediate L/r columns; Ylinen's equation (Eq. 9-29) with c = 0.8 fits solid-sawn and glulam, c = 0.9 structural composite lumber; c = 0.957 matches the fourth-power formula (p. 9-14)
Built-up columns: Eq. 9-30 with Kf = 0.75 for bolts, 0.6 for nails, provided spacing requirements meet design specification approval (p. 9-14)
Thin outstanding flanges: fcr = 0.044 E t^2/b^2, Eq. 9-31; up to 1.6 times with glued, filleted joints (p. 9-14, 9-15)
sections.applicability: Column (post, stud, brace) buckling capacity checks, including built-up/spaced columns and thin-flange built-up sections.

sections.title: Stability Equations: Bending (Water Ponding, Lateral-Torsional Buckling, Deck Support)
sections.summary: Beam instability: critical ponding spacing scr = m pi^4 E I/(rho L^4) (Eq. 9-32; rho printed as the density of water, 1,000 kg m^-3; as printed; see the note in the body: scr needs the unit weight, 9,810 N m^-3); lateral-torsional buckling of long rectangular beams fb_cr = pi^2 EL/alpha^2 (Eq. 9-33) with the slenderness factor alpha (Eq. 9-34) and Table 9-2's effective lengths; short beams by Figure 9-18; deck support by Figure 9-23 with tau = s GD L^2/EIy (Eq. 9-35).
sections.body: [p. 9-15] Beams are subject to two kinds of instability: lateral-torsional buckling and progressive deflection under water ponding, both of which are determined by member stiffness. Roof beams that are insufficiently stiff or spaced too far apart for their given stiffness can fail by progressive deflection under the weight of water (Fig. 9-21). According to Zahn (1988), the critical beam spacing is scr = m pi^4 E I/(rho L^4) (Eq. 9-32), where E is beam modulus of elasticity, I beam moment of inertia, rho density of water (1,000 kg m^-3, 0.0361 lb in^-3), L beam length, and m = 1 for simple support or m = 16/3 for fixed-end condition. To prevent ponding, the beam spacing must be less than scr. Print note: for scr to be a length, rho must be the weight of water per unit volume (9,810 N m^-3; the printed 0.0361 lb in^-3 is a weight density); with the printed 1,000 kg m^-3 the spacing comes out about 9.81 times too large. Lateral-torsional buckling: because most wood beams are rectangular in cross section, the equations are for rectangular members only; built-up I, H, and closed box sections are more stable than the equations would predict. Long slender beams that are restrained against torsional, axial rotation at their points of support but are otherwise free to twist and to deflect laterally will buckle when the maximum bending stress fb equals or exceeds fb_cr = pi^2 EL/alpha^2 (Eq. 9-33), [p. 9-16] where the slenderness factor is alpha = sqrt(2 pi) (EIy/GJ)^(1/4) sqrt(Le h)/b (Eq. 9-34), EIy is lateral flexural rigidity equal to EL h b^3/12, h beam depth, b beam width, GJ as defined in Equation (9-9), and Le the effective length determined by type of loading and support as given in Table 9-2 (conservative for beams with a width-to-depth ratio of less than 0.4; the load is assumed to act at the top edge of the beams). Equation (9-33) is valid for bending stresses below the proportional limit. Short beams can buckle at stresses beyond the proportional limit; it is recommended that short-beam buckling be analyzed by using the column buckling criterion in Figure 9-18 with alpha in place of L/r and fb_cr/Fb in place of fcr/Fc, Fb being beam modulus of rupture. Deck support: decking often provides enough restraint to prevent lateral-torsional buckling where it is attached to the compression edge. Where a beam is continuous over a support, the top edge is in tension and the deck provides no restraint to the compression edge; lateral bracing, such as diagonal blocking or a trussed diaphragm, must be added to bring lateral stability to the bottom, compression side, of the beam. Even if the deck flexes under in-plane shear, Equation (9-33) and Figure 9-18 can still be used if the effective length is divided by theta from Figure 9-23, whose abscissa is the deck shear stiffness parameter tau = s GD L^2/EIy (Eq. 9-35, Zahn 1973), where s is beam spacing, GD in-plane shear rigidity of deck, and L actual beam length. This figure applies only to simply supported beams. Cantilevers with the deck on top have their tension edge supported and do not derive much support from the deck.
key_points: Ponding: scr = m pi^4 E I/(rho L^4), Eq. 9-32, m = 1 simple, 16/3 fixed; beam spacing must be less than scr; rho is printed as 1,000 kg m^-3, but scr needs the unit weight (9,810 N m^-3 or 0.0361 lb in^-3) (p. 9-15)
Lateral-torsional buckling: fb_cr = pi^2 EL/alpha^2, Eq. 9-33, alpha = sqrt(2 pi)(EIy/GJ)^(1/4) sqrt(Le h)/b, Eq. 9-34, Le from Table 9-2; valid below the proportional limit (p. 9-15, 9-16)
Over a continuous support the deck restrains only the tension edge; lateral bracing must be added for the bottom compression side (p. 9-16)
Deck support: divide the effective length by theta from Figure 9-23, tau = s GD L^2/EIy (Eq. 9-35); simply supported beams only (p. 9-16)
sections.applicability: Roof-beam ponding stability, and lateral-torsional (out-of-plane) buckling stability of unbraced or partially braced beams.

sections.title: Interaction of Buckling Modes
sections.summary: When axial load, edgewise bending and flatwise bending act together, the combination can buckle even though each load is below its own critical value. Zahn's interaction equation (Eq. 9-36) with the moment magnification factors theta_c1 (Eq. 9-37) and theta_c2 (Eq. 9-38) and the elastic buckling stresses F''c1, F''c2 (Eq. 9-39, 9-40) and F''b1 = (1.44 E/le)(d2/d1) (Eq. 9-41; as printed; see the note in the body: the printed form does not give a stress).
sections.body: [p. 9-16] When two or more loads are acting and each of them has a critical value associated with a mode of buckling, the combination can produce buckling even though each load is less than its own critical value. The general case of a beam of unbraced length le includes a primary (edgewise) moment M1, a lateral (flatwise) moment M2, and axial load P. The axial load creates a secondary moment on both edgewise and flatwise moments due to the deflection under combined loading given by Equation (9-7). [p. 9-17] In addition, the edgewise moment has an effect like the secondary moment effect on the flatwise moment (Fig. 9-24). Based on Zahn (1986), the following equation contains two moment modification factors, one on the edgewise bending stress and one on the flatwise bending stress that includes the interaction of biaxial bending, and a squared term for axial load to better fit experimental data: (fc/F'c)^2 + [fb1 + 6(e1/d1) fc (1.234 - 0.234 theta_c1)]/(theta_c1 F'b1) + [fb2 + 6(e2/d2) fc (1.234 - 0.234 theta_c2)]/(theta_c2 Fb2) <= 1.0 (Eq. 9-36), where f is the member stress in compression, edgewise bending, or flatwise bending (subscripts c, b1, or b2), F buckling strength in compression or bending (a single prime denotes the strength is reduced for slenderness of the member; a double prime denotes the elastic buckling stress), e/d ratio of eccentricity of the axial compression to member depth for edgewise or flatwise bending (subscripts 1 or 2), and theta_c moment magnification factors for edgewise and flatwise bending, given by theta_c1 = 1 - (fc/F''c1 + s/scr) (Eq. 9-37) and theta_c2 = 1 - [fc/F''c2 + (fb1 + 6(e1/d1) fc)/F''b1] (Eq. 9-38), with F''c1 = 0.822 E/(le1/d1)^2 (Eq. 9-39), F''c2 = 0.822 E/(le2/d2)^2 (Eq. 9-40), and F''b1 = (1.44 E/le)(d2/d1) (Eq. 9-41), where le is effective length of member and s and scr are previously defined ponding beam spacing. Print note: as printed, the right side of Eq. 9-41 has the units of stress divided by length, not a stress; a dimensionally consistent form is 1.44 E d2^2/(le d1). Figure 9-24 shows a simply supported biaxial beam-column with laterally constrained end supports (le = le1 = le2); the effective spans le1 and le2 may change if interior vertical supports or lateral bracing is added. The 1-2 coordinate system denotes edgewise and flatwise bending. For more complex cases of combined loading, Zahn (1988) offers a detailed approach that may be adapted to more beam-column configurations.
key_points: Combined axial load and biaxial bending can buckle even when each load is below its own critical value (p. 9-16)
F''c1 = 0.822 E/(le1/d1)^2 (Eq. 9-39) and F''c2 = 0.822 E/(le2/d2)^2 (Eq. 9-40) for compression; edgewise bending F''b1 = (1.44 E/le)(d2/d1) as printed (Eq. 9-41), a different form (p. 9-17)
sections.applicability: The general biaxial beam-column check for members simultaneously carrying axial load, edgewise (strong-axis) bending, and flatwise (weak-axis) bending -- e.g., a wall stud also serving as a rafter tie or purlin.
